In this question, three sentences A, B and C are given. Decide which is/are correct with respect to grammar, meaning and usage and choose your answer accordingly.

A. AI assistants are primarily used as practiced tools to help with tasks such as writing, editing and sourcing information.                     
	B. Agriculture has entered a new scientific era.                     
	C. Banks are not unwilling to finance climate technologies; they are unwilling to finance risks they cannot adequately assess or price.

A. AI assistants are primarily used as practiced tools to help with tasks such as writing, editing and sourcing information.                             
	B. Agriculture has entered a new scientific era.                             
	C. Banks are not unwilling to finance climate technologies; they are unwilling to finance risks they cannot adequately assess or price.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below. Certain words are given in bold to help you  locate them while answering some of the questions.                                                         	
		‘Gen Z’ has emerged as one of the most talked — about terms in India in recent past. The spotlight on this generation reflects a growing recognition that its aspirations, choices and capabilities will                                                                                                               profoundly                                                                                                                      influence the country’s future. Yet an even bigger story is unfolding beyond the headlines. Gen Z is India’s first generation to step into higher education and the workplace in the age of AI. For the Baby Boomers, the defining technology was television. Generation X witnessed the rise of the personal computer. Millennials transformed the smartphone into an indispensable companion. Gen Z grew up in the age of social media, with platforms such as Instagram becoming integral to communication, creativity and self-expression. It is now the first generation to begin its professional journey alongside AI. Unlike earlier technological revolutions that unfolded over decades, AI is evolving at a remarkable speed. India is uniquely placed in this transformation. With one of the world’s youngest populations, the country possesses an extraordinary demographic advantage. Yet demographics alone do not guarantee prosperity. India’s demographic dividend will remain a statistic unless it is transformed into an economic and an AI dividend. That transformation will depend on whether its Gen Z are equipped to thrive in an AI-driven world.                                                                 	
		India’s digital public infrastructure, expanding startup ecosystem and growing adoption of AI across sectors provide fertile ground for innovation. If educational institutions, industry and policymakers work in concert, the country has an opportunity not merely to participate in the global AI revolution, but to help shape it. AI is already changing the nature of work. Routine tasks such as drafting documents, analysing large volumes of data, scheduling activities and generating basic content are increasingly being automated. Consequently, employers are beginning to value qualities that machines cannot easily replicate, like critical thinking, creativity, ethical judgement, learning agility and emotional intelligence. AI is not simply changing jobs; it is changing the skills that make people employable. The future belongs to those                                                                                                                               who can outthink AI.                                                                                                                                      This presents both an opportunity and a challenge for India’s Gen Z. Unlike earlier generations, today’s students have                                                                                                                                               unprecedented                                                                                                                                                      access to powerful AI tools that can explain concepts, summarize information, generate ideas and accelerate learning. However, frequent use of AI should not be mistaken for AI literacy. Knowing how to use an AI application is very different from knowing how to frame effective prompts, verify responses, recognise inaccuracies and apply AI thoughtfully. True AI literacy also means understanding AI’s limitations, recognising bias, safeguarding privacy and knowing when human judgement must prevail. AI should become a thinking partner, not a thinking substitute.
